title: Ezekiel 3:12–21
context: The Spirit lifts the prophet, and he hears behind him “the voice of a great rushing,” saying, “Blessed be the LORD’s glory from his place” (3:12), with the noise of the creatures’ wings and the wheels (3:13). He goes “in bitterness, in the heat of my spirit”, with the LORD’s hand strong on him (3:14), comes to the exiles “at Tel Aviv who lived by the river Chebar,” and sits “overwhelmed among them seven days” (3:15). The location of Tel Aviv in Babylonia is not known with certainty. At the end of seven days the LORD makes him “a watchman to the house of Israel” (3:17). Verses 18–21 set out four cases: the wicked not warned, the wicked warned, the righteous who turns and is not warned, and the righteous who is warned and does not sin. The charge concerns the prophet’s responsibility to warn and the hearer’s responsibility to turn, in the setting of his commissioning. It returns in Ezekiel 33:1–9, and the turning of the righteous and the wicked is developed in Ezekiel 18:21–28 and 33:10–20. Both traditions affirm the prophet’s duty and the hearer’s accountability. They read 3:20 with different emphases, and the wider question of whether a true believer may finally fall away is treated at Hebrews 6:4 and Hebrews 6:6; this page does not settle it here.

verses.text: Then the Spirit lifted me up, and I heard behind me the voice of a great rushing, saying, “Blessed be the LORD’s glory from his place.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Then the Spirit lifted me up,” and the prophet hears “Blessed be the LORD’s glory from his place.” Arminian readers note that the commissioning scene closes in praise. The glory that called the prophet is blessed, and the prophet is carried to his task.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear doxology at the close of the commission, giving glory to the LORD in his place. Shared ground: both traditions read the Spirit’s lifting as part of the visionary experience, not as a point of dispute, and both see the scene ending in praise.

verses.text: I heard the noise of the wings of the living creatures as they touched one another, and the noise of the wheels beside them, even the noise of a great rushing.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet hears “the noise of the wings of the living creatures as they touched one another,” and the wheels, “even the noise of a great rushing.” Arminian readers note that the sounds recall the vision of chapter 1. The same glory is present in power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the vision’s majesty recalled in sound (compare 1:24). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as tying the commission back to the throne-vision, so that the prophet goes out knowing who sent him.

verses.text: So the Spirit lifted me up, and took me away; and I went in bitterness, in the heat of my spirit; and the LORD’s hand was strong on me.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet goes “in bitterness, in the heat of my spirit; and the LORD’s hand was strong on me.” Arminian readers note the honest emotion of the servant. Readers differ on whether the bitterness is grief over the message, distress at the task, or something else.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the sweet scroll of 3:3 is followed by a bitter going, and they hold together the prophet’s anguish and the LORD’s strong hand. Shared ground: both traditions leave the exact cause of the bitterness open, since the text does not state it.

verses.text: Then I came to them of the captivity at Tel Aviv who lived by the river Chebar, and to where they lived; and I sat there overwhelmed among them seven days.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet comes to the exiles “at Tel Aviv who lived by the river Chebar” and sits “overwhelmed among them seven days.” Arminian readers note the solidarity of the messenger with his people. He sits among them before he speaks to them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a period of silent identification with the exiles, though the text does not explain the seven days. Shared ground: both traditions hedge the location of Tel Aviv and read the verse as the prophet entering the community he is called to serve.

verses.text: At the end of seven days, the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: “At the end of seven days, the LORD’s word came to me”. Arminian readers note that the prophet does not begin on his own initiative. He waits, and the word comes in the LORD’s time, bringing the watchman charge that follows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress that the prophetic word comes at God’s appointed time. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the transition from the prophet’s silent waiting among the exiles to the specific charge of 3:17–21.

verses.text: “Son of man, I have made you a watchman to the house of Israel. Therefore hear the word from my mouth, and warn them from me.
verses.arminianNotes: “Son of man, I have made you a watchman to the house of Israel.” Arminian readers note the image of a sentry who sees danger and sounds the alarm. The watchman is to “hear the word from my mouth, and warn them from me”, so the warning is the LORD’s own.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the prophet appointed by the LORD to warn on the LORD’s behalf. Shared ground: both traditions read the watchman as a sent messenger whose warning carries God’s authority, and both note that the charge returns in Ezekiel 33:1–9.

verses.text: When I tell the wicked, ‘You will surely die;’ and you give him no warning, nor speak to warn the wicked from his wicked way, to save his life, that wicked man will die in his iniquity; but I will require his blood at your hand.
verses.arminianNotes: If the prophet gives no warning “to save his life,” the wicked man “will die in his iniquity; but I will require his blood at your hand.” Arminian readers note the weight of the prophet’s responsibility. The wicked man is guilty, and the silent watchman is accountable too.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise affirm the prophet’s real accountability alongside the wicked man’s real guilt. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as joining two responsibilities, the prophet’s duty to warn and the hearer’s guilt for his way, without letting either cancel the other.

verses.text: Yet if you warn the wicked, and he doesn’t turn from his wickedness, nor from his wicked way, he will die in his iniquity; but you have delivered your soul.”
verses.arminianNotes: If the prophet warns and the wicked does not turn, “he will die in his iniquity; but you have delivered your soul.” Arminian readers note that the hearer’s refusal is his own. The warning offered a real way of escape, and rejecting it is culpable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the prophet freed from blame once he has faithfully warned, with the outcome resting on the hearer’s response under God’s governance. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as defining faithfulness by the warning given, not by the results achieved.

verses.text: “Again, when a righteous man turns from his righteousness and commits iniquity, and I lay a stumbling block before him, he will die. Because you have not given him warning, he will die in his sin, and his righteous deeds which he has done will not be remembered; but I will require his blood at your hand.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD warns that “when a righteous man turns from his righteousness and commits iniquity,” he will die, and “his righteous deeds which he has done will not be remembered”. Arminian readers commonly see a real righteousness that can be abandoned, so the warning describes a genuine possibility, and they often read the “stumbling block” as the LORD’s judicial response to a turning already chosen. How directly the verse speaks to final salvation, rather than to life and death within Ezekiel’s covenant setting, is debated. The wider question of falling away is treated at Hebrews 6:4 and Hebrews 6:6, and is not settled here.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers commonly read the righteousness here as outward or covenantal, or read the warning as one of the means by which God keeps his people persevering. They stress the LORD’s sovereign governance, including the “stumbling block”, alongside the person’s real guilt and the watchman’s real duty. Shared ground: both traditions take the warning seriously and hedge its application; the wider question of falling away is treated at Hebrews 6:4 and Hebrews 6:6, and is not settled here.

verses.text: Nevertheless if you warn the righteous man, that the righteous not sin, and he does not sin, he will surely live, because he took warning; and you have delivered your soul.”
verses.arminianNotes: If the prophet warns the righteous man and he does not sin, “he will surely live, because he took warning”. Arminian readers note that heeding the warning is the righteous person’s real response. The warning is effective as it is received and obeyed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the warning as a means by which God preserves the righteous, so that taking warning is the fruit of grace at work. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that warnings are meant for life, and that the faithful watchman is told, “you have delivered your soul.”
